profile.summary: This is the evaluation published with MetageNN, a long-read taxonomic classifier. Six tools assign Oxford Nanopore reads from 81 verified bacterial isolates to a genus, all of them indexing the same 516 reference genomes, in two settings: when the read's own species is in the database, and when it is not. The same tools are then run on 30 pseudo-mock communities built from the out-of-database isolates, and Table 1 records each tool's database size and classification speed. It is useful to someone choosing a read classifier and wanting to know how each behaves when the species is missing from the reference set.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Whether a tool can put a long read in the right genus, and what happens when the read's species has no genome in the reference database. The authors set the problem up around that gap: the SRA has Nanopore data for only 489 unique bacterial species while RefSeq had complete genomes for more than 6800, so a classifier is often asked about a species it has never seen. The second question is cost: how much disk the database needs and how many reads per second the tool classifies.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: The test data are real Nanopore reads with a checked ground truth. The authors searched the SRA for R.9.4.1 Nanopore datasets from bacterial isolates whose species had a RefSeq genome, confirmed the strain name matched, then assembled each read set with Flye and two rounds of medaka polishing and required average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference. That left 81 strains, subsampled to about 20,000 reads each. The 47 strains whose genome is in the reference set form the Species in the database set and the remaining 34 form the Species out of the database set. The main database is the 47 genomes expanded about tenfold with randomly chosen RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the repository's list of those assemblies has 516 lines. A smaller 47-genome database was used only for model and hyperparameter choices and for the comparison against other deep learning classifiers.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: Every tool indexes the same main database, and the non-machine-learning tools are run at their default settings. Reads are classified at genus rank and scored by sensitivity, precision and F1 per bacterial isolate, then averaged across isolates within a dataset; differences against MetageNN are tested with a Wilcoxon rank sum test. Error bars in the figures are the standard deviation across isolates. MetageNN itself was trained on 8x coverage of the main database genomes, about 17 million 1 kbp sequences, with 200 validation sequences per genome, and classifies a read by splitting it into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks and taking a majority vote, accepting a call only at probability 0.5 or above. GeNet was given a matched parameter count and the same training data so that the difference between the two is mainly how they encode a long read.

sections.title: The community-level test
sections.body: Thirty pseudo-mock communities were assembled from the reads of the out-of-database isolates, each with a random number of species between 20 and 34 and up to 100,000 reads log-distributed across them. Two things are reported: the percentage of reads a tool classifies, and sensitivity, precision and F1 for the presence or absence of a genus at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1% of the reads in the dataset, which is about 1, 100 and 1000 reads. GeNet was dropped from this comparison because of its performance in the read-level test. MetageNN classified 93.26% of the reads, ahead of MMseqs2 at 85.49%, Kraken2 at 64.90%, MEGAN-LR at 53.06% and MetaMaps at 37.30%.

MetageNN outperformed all existing tools classifying 93.26% of the reads from species out of the database at the genus level. This result was followed by MMseqs2, Kraken2, MEGAN-LR and MetaMaps with 85.49%, 64.90%, 53.06% and 37.30%, respectively.

sections.title: Reported results
sections.body: The two settings separate the tools. When the species is in the database, Kraken2, MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR have the best average F1, sensitivity and precision and beat MetageNN. When it is not, MetageNN has the highest sensitivity along with MMseqs2, improving on MetaMaps, Kraken2, GeNet and MEGAN-LR by 100%, 23%, 17% and 36%; its precision is slightly lower than MetaMaps, Kraken2 and MMseqs2, and only the gap to MEGAN-LR is significant. Over both sets together MMseqs2 is first on F1 and sensitivity with 0.85 and 0.81, then Kraken2 with 0.83 and 0.79. Every tool does worse when three or fewer species share the tested genus. Table 1 gives database size and speed: MetageNN uses 0.839 GB at 1424 reads per second, against 3.7 GB for Kraken2, 5.1 GB for MEGAN-LR and 27.8 GB for MMseqs2.

sections.title: How to run it
sections.body: The repository publishes the model code, the genome and isolate lists and the hyperparameter files, not the benchmark harness. Requirements are installed by a shell script. Sequences are turned into canonical 6-mer profiles with the Phylopythia k-mer counter, fasta2kmers2, and training is one command that reads a settings JSON. Only the small-database training set, at 1x coverage, is offered for download, through a link in the data folder; the main-database training data and the test read sets are not in the repository, only lists of the SRA identifiers and RefSeq assemblies they come from.
sections.source_locator: Repository: README.md, Requirements, Counting k-mers, Settings and Training; data/README.txt

python code/MetageNN_train.py -s settings/MetageNN_settings_small_database.json
A link is also provided to download the "small database" training dataset (1x coverage) that can be used to train MetageNN.
SRA isolates used (list_of_sra_ids_species_in.txt and list_of_sra_ids_species_out.txt) are publicly avalaible at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra

facts.label: Splits
facts.value: The split is by whether the test species is in the reference database, not by random sampling. Training sequences are 1 kbp windows sampled from the database genomes (8x coverage of the main database, about 17 million samples; 1x coverage of the small database, about 235,000 sequences), validation is 200 sequences per genome drawn the same way with different seeds, and the test reads are real Nanopore reads from isolates. The 34 out-of-database isolates have no genome in the database at all.

facts.label: Metrics
facts.value: Sensitivity, precision and F1 at genus rank, higher better, averaged across bacterial isolates for the read-level tests and across the 30 communities for the community-level test, where presence of a genus is decided at cumulative read thresholds of 0.001%, 0.1% and 1%. The community test also reports the percentage of reads classified, higher better. Table 1 reports database memory in GB, lower better, and speed in reads per second, higher better.

facts.label: Baselines
facts.value: Five classifiers beside MetageNN: MetaMaps and MEGAN-LR (alignment based, with minimap2 alignments for MEGAN-LR), MMseqs2 with a nucleotide database, Kraken2 for k-mer matching, and GeNet as the deep learning representative. DeepMicrobes and GeNet were also compared on the small database for training and inference cost and for robustness to simulated errors; GeNet was dropped from the community-level test.
facts.source_locator: Paper: Baselines (both sections); Results; Experimental setup for the pseudo-mock analysis

quotes.text: We selected five taxonomic classifiers that are representative of different approaches.
As alignment-based taxonomic classifiers methods designed for long-read technologies, we selected MetaMaps
Although a taxonomy classifier for metagenomic contigs, we also included MMseqs2 (nucleotide-based database)
As a representative of k-mer matching methods, we selected Kraken2
DeepMicrobes is based on recurrent neural networks, which means that for each k-mer it will perform forward and backward propagation.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: Two. The Species out of the database setting removes the test species' genome from the reference set altogether, and the results are further stratified by how many species share the tested genus (exactly one, two or three, more than three), which separates the easy cases from the hard ones. Within the model's own data, validation sequences are drawn with different seeds from the training sequences. Test reads are real reads whose identity was confirmed by assembly and an average nucleotide identity above 99% to the reference, so the ground truth does not come from the classifier under test.

gaps: The per-tool sensitivity, precision and F1 values are printed only on bar plots in Figures 3 and 4; no table or data file of them is published, so only the values quoted in the prose could be recorded.
No source read gives the number of reads in each test set after subsampling, only about 20,000 per isolate and a maximum of 100,000 per pseudo-mock community.
The repository states no licence, and the GitHub API reports none, so the terms for the code and the data lists are unknown.
The repository has no benchmark runner: the commands published cover k-mer counting and training MetageNN on the small database, not reproducing the comparison against the five baselines.

The settings file for the main database names a training array at 1x coverage with 236,212 samples, which does not match the paper's description of 8x coverage and about 17 million samples for the main-database model; the sources read do not resolve this.

notes: Written from the PMC full text (PMC11022314, CC BY 4.0) and five files of the csb5/MetageNN repository at commit d7c858cee1b88bf78fb1ea7d120b3be180a52b69. Points for a human. First, the repository states no licence and the GitHub API reports none, so code_licence and data_licence are null and the repository files are kept but not stored. Second, Table 1 prints Kraken2's speed as 13.471 reads per second, which reads like a thousands separator for 13,471 given that it is marked the best performer in that column; it is quoted as printed and not reinterpreted here. Third, the main-database settings file in the repository points at a 1x training array of 236,212 samples while the paper describes the main-database model as trained on 8x coverage and about 17 million samples, so the published settings file may not be the one behind the reported results. Fourth, the per-tool sensitivity, precision and F1 values are only in bar plots, so the entries here carry the metric and the split but the figures quoted are limited to those printed in the prose. Fifth, the released date is the PMC release date of 16 April 2024 printed in the article's publication history.
